newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl puts off coal crisis talks as miners protest.
newsitem.headline: Kohl puts off coal crisis talks as miners protest.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl postponed crisis talks with mining union leaders on Tuesday because of an atmosphere of intimidation created by thousands of angry pit workers who gathered in Bonn to protest at planned subsidy cuts.

Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl told reporters on the fringe of a cabinet meeting that "reasonable talks cannot be held in such a tense atmosphere". He said Kohl would meet Hans Berger, head of the IG Bergbau miners' union, on Thursday, but only if the miners ended their protest in Bonn.
Kohl himself told reporters: "I won't let myself be put under pressure as a matter of principle. I want us to make moves towards each other in reasonable talks."
But it was not clear if the 13,000 or so miners, who had defied their union to come to Bonn and virtually besieged the government quarter since Monday, would yield to such appeals.
Immediately after the news of the postponement hundreds forced their way through a police barricade into an exclusion zone shouting: "We're going to the chancellery!"

"No one has any prospects and we are very angry indeed," said one 34-year-old miner. "We don't think much of the principle of non-violent protest." Many others announced their intention to stay until Thursday.
Berger said Bonn was to blame for stoking up the protests, telling reporters: "The lack of readiness to compromise is likely to be seen as a provocation."
But at a rally he made a passionate appeal to the miners to return home, at least until Thursday.
"Don't let them steal the arguments. Protest in your regions and if no compromise is reached, we are ready to come back!"
The confrontation with the miners is perhaps the most dramatic sign yet of growing discontent with an apparently endless series of welfare cuts, budget savings and job losses.

In Berlin, a protest by more than 5,000 construction workers on the site of the new German parliament led to scuffles with police. The builders are angry about unemployment in the sector and the effect of cheaper foreign labour.

The government gave no sign that it was prepared to give ground to the miners, who stopped work in Germany's 18 pits on Friday after Bonn said it would cut subsidies to 3.8 billion marks by 2005 instead of the promised 6.5 billion.
Currently Bonn pays over nine billion marks a year to compensate users for a domestic coal price which is over three times the world market price.
IG Bergbau says the government plans will force 10 pits to close by 2005, make 50,000 miners redundant and cause a further 70,000 related job losses in already depressed areas.

Buses poured into Bonn all night from the Ruhr, Germany's ailing steel-and-coal heartland, and from Saar state on the French border where miners have blocked the main road routes to Luxembourg for four days.
Other miners chained themselves overnight to the Bonn headquarters of the free-market Free Democrats FDP, Kohl's junior coalition partners and the driving force behind the cuts.
When the miners heard news of the postponement, they began chanting "Cowardly pigs!" and hurling eggs at the FDP building, which they have blocked since Monday.
But Bohl, a member of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), told reporters the government's offer was "fair and comprehensive".
Economics Minister Guenther Rexrodt of the FDP said there was scant room to compromise when each mining job cost the government 130,000 marks ($76,200) a year.

"Our offer means we are providing more than 50 billion marks for the mining sector over nine years," he told German Radio. "Coal subsidies have been declining for many decades, and it was well known that there would be a cut in 1997 of the order that has been proposed."
